checkpoints: Selecting every row from `documents` with no `ORDER BY` and no `LIMIT` forces the full table — id, content, and every embedding vector — to be pulled out of Postgres and shipped over the wire on each retrieval call.

Computing `cosineSimilarity` in application code once per row is an O(n) scan across the entire corpus for every single query, and sorting all of those scored rows in memory before slicing the top 3 wastes work on rows that get thrown away.

This pattern is invisible at a handful of seed documents because the data volume and scan cost are both trivial, but it degrades badly as the corpus grows into the hundreds of thousands of chunks — the LLM call is not the bottleneck, the network transfer and the app-side scan are.

The first-stage fix is to move the nearest-neighbour search into the database itself: query with `ORDER BY embedding <=> $1::vector LIMIT $2` using pgvector's cosine-distance operator, so Postgres does the ranking and only the top-k rows ever cross the wire.

The similarity-to-score conversion (`1 - distance`) and the `SIMILARITY_THRESHOLD` filter should still be applied, but only to the k rows the database returns, not to the whole corpus — the app-side `cosineSimilarity` and `parseVectorLiteral` helpers drop out of the request path entirely once the query does the work.

An approximate nearest-neighbour index such as HNSW or IVFFlat should only be introduced once the exact in-database scan itself becomes the bottleneck at very large scale — it is a second-stage optimization, not an automatic first move.

Adding an ANN index trades exactness for speed: the neighbours returned become approximate rather than guaranteed top-k, so the recall loss versus the latency gain is a judged trade-off rather than a free win.

Verifying the change means measuring p95 query latency before and after at a realistic corpus size, running `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` to confirm the query plan actually uses the index once one exists, checking retrieval quality hasn't silently regressed by comparing approximate results against an exact scan on a sample of queries, and re-running the grounded and fallback end-to-end flows to confirm answers still cite the right chunks.

User-perceived latency in a streaming response is governed by time-to-first-token, not total generation time — the two are independent, and a fix that shortens total generation time without moving the first byte earlier does nothing for perceived latency.

Setting `Content-Type: text/event-stream` and shaping each event correctly makes an endpoint look like it streams, but the actual guarantee of streaming is that bytes cross the socket as each token is produced — correct framing and early delivery are separate properties, and only the second one fixes a blank-screen wait.

Pushing each formatted token into an in-memory array (or string) inside a `for await` loop and calling `res.write` only once after the loop exits collapses time-to-first-token to the full generation duration, because nothing reaches the client until every token has already been generated.

A client's request status can flip to 'streaming' the instant the HTTP response opens, independent of whether the server has written any data yet — so status alone does not prove data is arriving, and a blank screen with status already 'streaming' points at server-side buffering rather than a client-side issue.

Fixing the in-memory accumulation bug is not sufficient on its own: headers set via `setHeader` are not guaranteed to reach the client until the first write or an explicit flush, so calling `res.flushHeaders()` right after setting headers is needed for the client to see the connection open before the first token arrives.

Without a `Cache-Control: no-cache, no-transform` response header (and, behind nginx specifically, `X-Accel-Buffering: no`), an intermediate reverse proxy or CDN is free to buffer correctly-flushed per-token writes and release them together later — so the server-side fix and the anti-buffering header are two independent, both-required fixes for the same symptom.

The correct fix moves the write inside the loop: each token is written and flushed to the response the moment it is produced, with no accumulating array or string kept — only a running counter is needed to report the total token count in the terminal 'done' event.

Verifying a streaming fix requires more than reading the code: asserting that response output grows while status is still 'streaming', measuring time-to-first-token before and after the fix, and re-running that check through the actual reverse proxy or CDN in front of the service — since a local request bypasses proxy-level buffering and cannot reveal it.

An SSE streaming handler has two independent lifecycles running side by side — the HTTP connection to the client and the token-generation loop pulling from the provider — and nothing links them unless code explicitly bridges the two.

An AbortController that is instantiated and correctly threaded into a provider's streamCompletion(...) call is not sufficient on its own; the controller only stops generation once something actually calls .abort() on it.

A framework does not automatically translate a client-side disconnect (closing the tab, tearing down a fetch) into an abort signal — that translation requires an explicit listener such as req.on("close", () => abortController.abort()).

Without a close-listener wired to the abort controller, abortController.signal.aborted never flips to true, so a for-await loop over the provider stream keeps pulling and writing tokens until the provider naturally finishes, even though the client already left.

Writing SSE frames to a connection nobody is reading and letting generation run to completion after a disconnect means that, with a real provider, the full completion still gets billed even though the response is discarded.

The fix requires two things together: registering an abort trigger on the connection's close event (or an equivalent request-scoped cancellation token/context the platform ties to the connection) and continuing to pass that same abort signal into the provider call exactly as before.

Checking abortController.signal.aborted before each write inside the streaming loop lets the loop break out immediately on cancellation rather than waiting for the next token from the provider, and that same check should guard against sending a terminal "done" frame after an abort.

Correct verification for this kind of fix is starting a stream, aborting after the first token, and confirming the server log stops at a low token count with an aborted/warning line and no "done" event — instead of continuing on to the full token count as if the client never left.

pgvector's `<=>` cosine-distance operator returns a value where a SMALLER number means the two vectors are more alike (0 for identical direction), which is the opposite of what a similarity score means.
Similarity is derived from distance as `1 - distance`, so it points the opposite direction from distance: a LARGER similarity value means more relevant, not less.

In `searchSimilar`, the SELECT projects `embedding <=> $1::vector AS score`, handing `score` the raw distance value, while `.filter((chunk) => chunk.score >= SIMILARITY_THRESHOLD)` is written as if `score` were a similarity — comparing a distance with `>=` against a similarity threshold inverts relevance.

This single inversion produces both symptoms at once: an on-topic chunk with a tiny distance (e.g. ~0.05) fails `0.05 >= 0.3`, gets filtered out, leaves zero chunks, and forces the `grounded=false` fallback even though the right document was retrieved.

An off-topic, near-orthogonal chunk with a large distance (e.g. ~0.6) passes `0.6 >= 0.3`, survives the filter, gets fed into the augmented prompt, and causes the LLM to answer confidently while citing an unrelated document.

`ORDER BY embedding <=> $1::vector` ranks strictly by ascending distance, so the closest chunk is always first before `LIMIT` cuts the top-k — the ordering logic is correct and is not the source of either bug.

The fix restores the missing distance-to-similarity conversion, e.g. rewriting the projection as `1 - (embedding <=> $1::vector) AS score` inside the same SQL query with no application-layer change needed, while the `ORDER BY` clause and the `>=` comparison stay untouched since only the meaning of `score` needs to change.

Proving the fix closes both bug reports requires an e2e regression pair rather than a single test: a known on-topic query must return `grounded: true` with the expected citation, and a known off-topic query must return `grounded: false` with empty citations, since testing only one direction would not catch the inversion resurfacing.

A guard that protects an expensive call must run as an admission check before that call executes, not as a report computed after the call already happened - a check placed after the provider call has already spent the money it was supposed to prevent spending.

In this handler, `this.cost.priceOf(result)` runs and `this.spentDollars` is updated right after `completion.complete(prompt)` returns, and only afterward is `spentDollars` compared against `budgetLimitDollars` - so the provider call and its cost are always paid before the budget is checked, guaranteeing the cap is overshot by at least one full paid request every time it is crossed.

Because the rejection only fires after the spend already happened, the caller whose request actually pushed spending over the budget still gets served in full; only their next request receives the 429 - enforcement lags one request behind the violation it is meant to prevent.

The fix is to turn the budget check into an admission gate: read the accumulated spend, compare it to the limit, and throw `429 BUDGET_EXCEEDED` (with the spent and limit figures in the response body) before `completion.complete` is ever invoked, the same way the rate-limit check already runs ahead of the handler's real work.

`remainingRequests` is a single field on the service instance with no `userId` anywhere near it, so every caller shares the same counter - one user issuing enough requests can exhaust the allowance meant for the entire user base, leaving everyone else rate-limited by someone else's traffic.

Per-user rate limiting requires keying the counter by `userId` (e.g. a `Map<string, Bucket>` token bucket); once the service runs more than one replica, that state can no longer live on `this` - each instance would keep its own counter and silently multiply the real limit by the replica count, so the bucket state has to move to a shared store like Redis with an atomic refill-and-consume operation.

`spentDollars` accumulates as a floating-point dollar amount on every call (`+= costDollars`), and floating-point addition of many small fractional values drifts away from the true total over time, so the number the budget guard compares against the limit can quietly disagree with what was actually billed.

Money should be accumulated as an integer unit such as micro-USD (`spentMicroUsd += 660`) rather than a float, since integer arithmetic has no rounding drift and keeps the figure the budget guard reads and the figure the cost log reports as one consistent, drift-free source of truth.
